text: The clinic hours run long and the public duties run longer, and somewhere behind them is a son whose birthday is coming. Dr. Alam is a neurologist and surgeon of standing, which in practice means a diary other people fill in for him. On the night of the birthday he learns something about the boy's health, and the man who spends his days reading other people's symptoms sets out to find his own child. Reza Mirkarimi takes two hours over that search, and the length does the work: it moves Alam out of the rooms where he is competent and deferred to, into places where he is one more person asking after someone. What accumulates is not guilt exactly. It is the arithmetic of how much of a man can be handed over to his profession before what is left of him is a stranger at his own table.

The meat in a shop window has to look a certain way, and somebody is paid badly to make it look that way. Hermógenes comes down from northern Argentina to Buenos Aires with a young wife, and takes work as an apprentice butcher for a man whose arrangements the trade knows about and does not discuss. Sebastián Schindel runs the film on two tracks — the shop, and the courtroom that follows the killing — and the second spends ninety-eight minutes asking the first to account for itself. Almost everything on screen is drawn from documented practice in the meat business rather than invented for effect. That sourcing changes what the film is: less a case study in one man's breaking point than a description of conditions that were in place long before he walked in.

Outside his own front door the boy is called Ernesto, and he is good at it. At home he is Juan; his mother, his father and his uncle Beto also carry more than one name, because in the Argentina of 1979 what the family does cannot be said out loud at school. Then there is María, who has only the one name, and who is the first thing in his life he did not inherit. Benjamín Ávila works from events he can vouch for and keeps the film at the boy's height, so the danger arrives sideways — in what adults decide not to explain, in the concentration a child brings to a lie he has been trained to tell. That costs the film every opportunity for a speech and buys something better: a first romance conducted under an alias is still a first romance, and he is entirely serious about it.

The war is nearly over, which is the worst possible time to be handed a position to hold. Ninety-three minutes, one battalion, one strait: Bahram Tavakkoli puts the Ammar battalion at Abughoraib in the closing days of the Iran-Iraq war, and a combat film that begins this late has already surrendered the turning point. Nothing settled here will move a line on any map, and the men can do that arithmetic themselves. What remains is duration and proximity — ammunition counted, ground measured in meters, the specific noise of a place that has a name only because of what is happening in it. An ending the audience already knows takes suspense off the table, which leaves the hours themselves, and the people obliged to fill them, to carry the whole thing.

Thirty-three years is long enough for a country to rearrange itself completely, and Bill Miner walks out into the result in 1901. The Pinkertons had filed him as the Gentleman Bandit, and the manners were not a cover story: he is courteous, easy company, and equipped for precisely one line of work, which the century has begun to leave behind. Phillip Borsos gives him ninety-two minutes and never once asks the audience to disapprove. The comedy and the sadness come from the same fact — a competent man with nothing left to be competent at, going back to robbery because it is the only thing that gives his days a shape. It is a western built at the pace of someone handed his life back who can think of one use for it.

The plan is the mother's: her son will run a marathon, and that will settle something. Cho-won is autistic, draws zebras, likes to run, and is already happy in a way that asks nobody's permission; what his mother wants is happiness other people can recognize, which is not the same thing at all. That gap is where the film lives. Chung Yoon-chul hands the training to a coach serving out an exile of his own, so the sessions never soften into encouragement, and the two hours stay close to the household — the long argument a family conducts with itself about what counts as a life going well. When the running finally comes it is not standing in for anything. It is a young man doing the one thing he was doing before anyone assigned it to him.

The rules are never stated out loud, and Emma sets about mastering them anyway. She meets Cassandra, and what starts between them is part friendship and part contest, physical, with each dare a small increase on the one before. Lisa Aschan gives it eighty-four minutes and supplies no motive, which is the right call: a film like this goes slack the moment it explains itself. What she films instead is the negotiation between two people competing to be the one who does not flinch, and the way that competition organizes everything else in their days. The pull for Emma is not Cassandra. It is the sensation of holding the whole arrangement steady, treated here as an appetite rather than a defect, which is why the escalation always has somewhere further to go.

The father has staked the family's future on his son's soccer, which is to say on a run of luck no one can guarantee. They are a Black middle-class family in Brazil, and the country has just elected a far-right president; Gabriel Martins declines to make that the story and arranges everything around it. The mother, after an encounter she cannot explain, becomes convinced she is under a curse. Whether the son wants any of what is being planned for him is a question the household has not scheduled time for. What gives the film its texture over 115 minutes is how much room each person's private project gets — this is less a family unit than several separate negotiations happening in the same set of rooms, conducted politely, mostly at cross purposes.

A film gets made about one particular officer for reasons that exist before the film does. Ahmad Motevaselian was an IRGC officer who commanded during the Iran-Iraq war, and Mohammad Hossein Mahdavian takes the whole life rather than a single operation, which sets the terms: a career will not fit in ninety-eight minutes, so what arrives is a run of episodes ordered by hindsight, with the audience supplying the connective tissue out of what it already believes. That is the standing difficulty of the commemorative portrait. The subject is not in dispute, which means the film cannot generate much by argument. It is also where such a picture can surprise, in the unremarkable stretches between the events that made the man worth commemorating in the first place.

The amusement park is to be called Deutschneyland, and the German businessman behind it wants a stretch of southern Sweden to put it on. Not all the locals are willing. Among the objectors is the Lindberg family, whose methods of obstruction are magical in the literal sense, and the joke depends on the delivery staying level: land deals, municipal enthusiasm and outright enchantment all treated as the same order of event. The Lindbergs' talents are never explained and do not need to be, since a comedy that files magic as one more local resource has solved its tonal problem in advance. Tage Danielsson had 103 minutes and a premise that is really an argument over a piece of countryside and what someone is willing to pay for it.

The rubber is contraband before the boy ever gets his hands on it. Roland's mother sells condoms under the counter in 1920s Stockholm, where the trade is against the law; Roland works out that the same stock makes slingshots, and goes into business. The household is an arrangement of positions — a socialist father, a Jewish mother, a brother who boxes — and the boy's discovery is that each of them, viewed from a certain angle, is also an opportunity. Åke Sandgren keeps the register between comedy and something harder. A schoolteacher has settled on Roland as the one who gets punished, which is the sort of attention no amount of good behavior escapes, so the boy answers the only way available to him: he finds another trade, and then another, and prices them.

Nothing leading up to it looks like the beginning of a murder case. Shimizu Yuichi is a day laborer, shy, and lonely in the specific way of a man who has routed his search for company through a telephone dating service. One of the women he met that way, Ishibashi Yoshino, is dead, and he is inside the event. Sang-il Lee takes 139 minutes over it, far longer than the crime needs, and the surplus goes to the surrounding hours: the work people do, the long drives, the small cruelties handed out and absorbed and never mentioned again. Yoshino is granted the same treatment, with her own contempt to dispense before any of this began. Everyone here was, that week, doing something entirely ordinary.

Seventy-eight minutes is a very short film to make about a condition measured in decades. Uje had his pop career in the 1990s; the diagnosis is Parkinson's, and Henrik Schyffert stays with the days rather than the prognosis — what a body will and will not do on a given morning, and what the people around it do with that. The film is filed as comedy as much as drama, and the comedy is not relief from the subject; it is the register the household actually speaks in. The brevity is a position. A longer film would have had to build toward something, and this one refuses to arrange a life into a shape while the person is still in the middle of living it. Nobody in it is required to be brave on schedule.

An accusation on a crowded train takes a second; what follows it takes 143 minutes, most of them indoors. A young man is charged with molesting a high-school girl, says he did not do it, and meets the machinery — arrest, detention, hearings that adjourn and resume, a procedure whose questions are not quite the question he keeps answering. A film that gives this much time to process has already refused the decisive exhibit and the closing speech; what Masayuki Suō puts in their place is forms, waiting, the calendar, the small daily cost of insisting on a word. The apparatus convenes around one contested moment and then does not disperse. The disproportion is the argument, and 143 minutes is how it gets made.
